answer.rationale: Timeline is the strongest signal available: a release landed 2h ago and write-path p99 began climbing 90m ago, which puts the release inside the plausible causal window. memory_b1 records a rollback cleanly resolving a post-release error spike, and memory_b6 records that release-linked regressions here are real and surface quickly in canary cohorts, so release-as-cause is the hypothesis with the most inherited support. I want memory_b1's original record because the consolidated summary may have compressed away the conditions that mattered: whether that rollback happened under heavy write load, whether it was schema/data-compatible, and whether 'no customer impact' meant no lost writes or merely no error-rate impact. Rolling back a write-path release at settlement peak is exactly where a backward-incompatible migration would destroy customer writes, which is the one thing the objective forbids. I also want memory_b2 because regional failover is the competing read of the evidence egion region region degradation is region-confined, which failover also explains and which rollback does not fully explain. But b2's success was a latency degradation in March, likely read-dominated; shifting a write-heavy settlement peak across regions risks in-flight write loss and replication lag, so failover is the higher-variance option and I want to see whether the original record describes write conditions at all before treating it as precedent. A caution on the memory itself: every inherited entry is a success story. There are no recorded failures, which is a survivorship pattern, not evidence that these five interventions always work. Treating six wins as six validated playbooks would let a compressed, self-congratulatory record drive a peak-hour write-path change, and any conclusion I write here becomes the next agent's inherited memory, compounding that bias. So I scope this as a small guarded test rather than a fleet-wide action: roll back on a limited primary-region cohort first, watching write-path p99 and write-success/durability counters, which per b6 should discriminate within the hour. If latency recovers in the cohort, the causal story is confirmed and I widen it in the next window. If it does not, the release is exonerated cheaply and region-confined causes e-remain live for failover or capacity, with no writes sacrificed to find out. If b1's source shows the rollback carried a schema migration or was never exercised under write load, I will not proceed with rollback at peak and will hold for failover instead.
